clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia defined by a locus on the long arm of chromosome 3 (3q27-q28); unlike most modern subtypes the causative gene remains unidentified.
Characterised by a triad of spastic paraparesis, mild intellectual disability and a distal motor neuropathy.
Adult-onset lower-limb spasticity was the presenting feature in the originally reported consanguineous kindred.
The distal motor neuropathy produces motor-predominant wasting and weakness of the feet, distinguishing SPG14 from purely corticospinal subtypes.
It remains a locus-defined entity, so the working diagnosis is largely one of exclusion supported by pedigree and linkage rather than a specific molecular test.
Recessive inheritance means parents are usually unaffected carriers, and a history of consanguinity should raise the index of suspicion.
Cerebellar signs, optic atrophy and a thin corpus callosum are not characteristic, helping to separate it from SPG7, SPG11 and SPG15.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG14 is defined by autosomal recessive linkage to a region on the long arm of chromosome 3 (3q27-q28); the specific disease gene and its protein product have not been established, so the underlying molecular mechanism remains unresolved. The clinical phenotype combines corticospinal (upper motor neurone) dysfunction with a distal motor axonal neuropathy, indicating disruption of a pathway important for maintaining both the long descending motor tracts and peripheral motor axons - a pattern shared with other motor-predominant complicated HSPs, but with the precise cellular defect awaiting gene identification. Because the condition has been described in only a small number of families, genotype-phenotype correlation is incompletely characterised.
additionalDifferentials: SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (ZFYVE26 / spastizin) - common recessive complicated HSPs with cognitive impairment and a thin corpus callosum
SPG7 (paraplegin) - recessive HSP with possible neuropathy and cerebellar or optic features
Pure dominant forms such as SPG4 and SPG3A, when the neuropathy or cognitive change is overlooked
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease with pyramidal signs (distal motor neuropathy mimic)
Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias with spasticity, including ARSACS
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing (given the absence of a specific gene test) with autozygosity/homozygosity mapping in consanguineous pedigrees
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to confirm the distal motor neuropathy
MRI of the brain and spine to assess for a thin corpus callosum, white-matter change and cord atrophy
Neuropsychometric assessment to characterise the intellectual disability
Metabolic and vitamin screen to exclude acquired myelo-neuropathy mimics
redFlags: Prominent early cognitive regression, a thin corpus callosum or leukoencephalopathy suggesting SPG11 or SPG15 rather than SPG14
Sensory ataxia or optic atrophy pointing to an alternative recessive syndrome
Rapid progression or a sensory level and sphincter disturbance indicating an acquired myelopathy
reference.prognosis: Slowly progressive, with disability arising from combined spasticity and distal motor weakness; prognostic data are limited given the small number of reported families.
pitfalls: Expecting a confirmatory single-gene test - SPG14 is currently locus-defined, so diagnosis leans on phenotype, pedigree and exclusion
Overlooking the distal motor neuropathy and misclassifying the case as a pure HSP
Conflating SPG14 with other cognitively complicated recessive forms without linkage or genomic support
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical review and classification
management: No gene-directed treatment is available; manage lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin for troublesome focal hypertonia
Physiotherapy, stretching and orthotic support tailored to the combined spastic weakness and distal motor-neuropathic wasting of the feet
Educational and neuropsychological support for the associated mild intellectual disability
Podiatry, orthopaedic and orthotic input for distal amyotrophy and foot deformity
Monitor mobility, contractures and neuropathic progression with periodic rehabilitation review and walking-aid provision
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with carrier testing of relatives and discussion of consanguinity-related recurrence risk
Escalate to multidisciplinary neurology and rehabilitation as combined spasticity and distal weakness advance
